sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**

All eight checklist lines are yes. One finding from reading the copy has no checklist line:

1. *(Off the checklist: copy the viewer will act on)* The times are vague. They sit at about 120–805, 148–245 in the first paragraph and 120–805, 412–477 in the third: "between early morning and late evening", "the last crossing leaves the quay before dusk", "one boat each hour". Someone reading "Notes for ferry passengers" wants to know whether they can catch a boat. The page tells them how often boats run but never when the first one leaves or the last one comes back. "Before dusk" moves through the winter, so a reader can't tell if a 4:30 pm crossing is still running. That gap is how people get stranded on the far bank. The page then sends them to "printed timetables… in the shelter at each landing", which only helps once they are already standing at the landing. The fix: give the first and last sailing from each side for summer and winter, or say when the winter timetable starts and link to the timetable itself. This is a defect (common sense, since no catalog entry covers it). Major, because the times are the piece's main job.

**What's working.**
- It's clear at once what the page is for. The bold sans headline at 120, 66–106 names its reader, and each paragraph covers one topic: the crossing, bicycles, winter. A first-time reader can sum it up in one sentence without effort.
- The plain styling suits the message. It's one column with near-black type on white and a sans heading over serif body text, with no decoration, which reads as a calm public notice. There's nothing on the page a reader would miss if it were gone.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

Bash was denied, so I couldn't run the crop script. At about 1280×800 the image is one screen, so I worked from the whole image.

**Walk (working notes)**
- First read: the eye lands on the bold sans title "Notes for ferry passengers" at top left (about x 120–593, y 68–104). Then it drops into three serif paragraphs of the same weight. It reads as a plain, calm notice page for ferry riders.
- Job (my assumption): an information page that tells passengers how the ferry runs, including times, bicycles and winter service.
- One element dominates: **yes**. The title looks about 38 px bold sans and the body about 20 px regular serif, so the eye knows where to start.
- Levels distinct, no near-equal sizes: **yes**. There are only two levels, title and body, and they are far apart in size.
- Headings differ beyond size: **yes**. The title differs from the body in weight (bold vs regular) and in form (sans vs serif).

No line was `no` or `unsure`, so step 5 (the deep read of entries) did not apply.

---

2. The title and body differ in three ways at once: size, weight, and sans vs serif. Because of that the two levels can't be confused, even though the piece uses only two. That fits a short notice; adding sizes would only add noise.

sections.report:
**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** No. The heading and the three paragraphs fill a block from about x 120–810 and y 65–490. To its right is an empty band about 470 px wide (x ≈ 810–1280), and below it about 310 px of empty space (y ≈ 490–800). All the weight sits in the top-left of the frame and nothing on the right or at the bottom balances it. On a wide screen the page looks pinned into a corner, more like an unstyled document or a page that hasn't finished loading than a designed notice, and the viewer's eye keeps going to the blank right side. Arnheim (*Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance") says a heavy side needs a counterweight. Fix: either centre the reading column in the viewport so the empty space is shared evenly on both sides, or use the right-hand field for something that belongs there and that the copy already mentions, such as the timetable or the landing times as a sidebar. The left-anchored column is a common web convention and the column itself works well, so this is a minor finding. Marked convention (Arnheim), with a taste element in how much it costs here. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The alignment is exact. The heading and all three paragraphs share one left edge at x≈120, with no near-misses, so the page reads as one calm column.
- Spacing shows the structure. The gap between paragraphs (about 20 px on top of the 32 px line spacing) is clearly larger than the line spacing, so each paragraph reads as its own topic: timings, bicycles, winter. The larger gap under the heading ties it to the body as a whole. The white space is also in one large area rather than spread thin between elements, which suits a short notice.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** How the column behaves at other viewport widths. The empty right side may only show up on wide screens. Check whether the column centres or stays pinned left at 1280 px and above.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (visual weight balances)

**Section.** Text: applies. The image is a 1280 × 800 page with one heading and three short paragraphs of body text.

**Findings**
None. Every line in the Text checklist is yes. Two notes for the director:
- **Lines that came close.** The body lines look like about 65 to 70 characters each (first line, x 120–775, about 68), so they fit the 45 to 75 range. The heading "Notes for ferry passengers" (x 120–593, y 68–105) looks set at the font's default letter spacing, not tightened. At about 40 px in a bold grotesque this still reads evenly, with no gaps or collisions in "passengers", so I answered yes.
- **A copy issue the checklist doesn't cover.** For a ferry notice the times are what readers act on, and the copy gives none: "between early morning and late evening", "the last crossing leaves the quay before dusk". A passenger can't plan around "early morning", and in winter "before dusk" changes from week to week. The only timetable it points to is the printed one in the shelter at each landing, which you can only read once you're already there. This is a defect for anyone planning a trip. The fix is to give the first and last sailing times, or link the timetable. Weight: major if the page's job is helping people plan crossings, minor if it's only general orientation.

**What's working.**
- **Clear pairing and good reading setup.** The heading is a bold sans and the body a serif made for reading, two plainly different faces with one job each. The body looks about 20 px, has open line spacing (about 32 px line to line) that suits the roughly 68-character lines, and is flush left with a gentle rag. It reads comfortably.
- **Paragraphs are marked once.** Each paragraph is separated only by space (about 20 px), with no indents, and the first paragraph starts flush under the heading. No paragraph ends on a single short word: the last lines are "tide turns against the boat.", "side of the deck." and "each landing.". The three short blocks break up the text naturally.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Color: applies. The page is all neutrals, with near-black text on a white background and no accent hue.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.** The heading (y ≈ 65–105) and the body text (x 120–810, y ≈ 140–490) are dark gray, close to black, on white. That gives strong contrast with no glare, so the text reads easily. All the structure comes from value and weight, so it holds up exactly the same in grayscale. Nothing on the page calls for color, such as a link, a status or a marked item. Leaving out an accent is the right choice for a plain block of notes for passengers.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

There's no broken-image icon or placeholder box, so I can't tell whether a picture, such as a route map or a photo of the ferry, was meant to go there and didn't load.
